learningObjective: Identify examples of operator-level IRs used in production and the features that characterize them.

canonicalClaims.claim: Operator-level (graph-level) IRs represent computations as coarse-grained ops on typed values with shape/dtype annotations; examples include XLA HLO / StableHLO, ONNX, TVM Relax, and PyTorch FX. Graph-level passes commonly include shape inference, constant folding, algebraic simplification, layout choice, and operator fusion.
conditions: The IR treats ops as atomic units without exposing loop iteration variables.
nonImplications: Does not imply operator-level IRs are strictly weaker than loop-level IRs; they compose across layers.
Does not imply the same set of graph-level passes runs in every framework.

misconceptions.claim: Operator-level IRs expose loop iteration variables.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Exposing iteration is the defining feature of loop-level (or tensor-expression) IRs.

misconceptions.claim: Operator-level IRs cannot perform any optimization; only loop-level IRs can.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Fusion, constant folding, and shape/layout optimization are canonical operator-level passes.

misconceptions.claim: ONNX is a loop-level IR because ONNX ops call vendor kernels.
misconceptions.whyWrong: ONNX is an operator-level interchange IR; runtime kernel invocation is a downstream concern.

misconceptions.claim: FX Graph is a low-level assembly IR.
misconceptions.whyWrong: FX Graph is an operator-level graph representation of Python-traced ATen ops.

implementationFacts: HLO / StableHLO: static / dynamic tensor types with per-op shape
Relax and FX: dynamic Python-side operator graphs
performanceScenarios: Graph-level operator IRs are the natural place for cross-op decisions (fusion, layout) before lowering.
